The occasion of its revelation is what al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) dispatched twenty-four men from his companions to Banu 'Amir, and they killed them, except for three who lagged behind them, so they were safe and returned to Madinah. The Almighty said: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers...﴾ up to the end of the verse.

Scholars differed about the occasion of its revelation. Ma'mar related from Qatadah that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and called out to him from behind the chamber: "O Muhammad, my praise is an adornment and my blame is a disgrace." The Prophet (ﷺ) came out and said: "Woe to you! That is God, that is God." Then God revealed this verse. This is one opinion.

Zayd ibn Arqam related: "Some people came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Come, let us go to this man. If he is a prophet, we are the happiest of people in following him, and if he is a king, we will live in his protection.' They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and began calling out to him while he was in his chamber, 'O Muhammad!' So God revealed this verse."

It has been said that they were from the Banu Tamim.

Muqatil said: They were nine men: Qays ibn 'Asim, al-Zibriqan ibn Badr, al-Aqra' ibn Habis, Suwayd ibn Hisham, Khalid ibn Malik, 'Ata' ibn Habis, al-Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad, Waki' ibn Waki', and 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn.

Regarding His saying ﴿Most of them do not understand﴾ there are two interpretations:

First: They do not know. He expressed knowledge by "understanding" because it is one of its results. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Second: They do not understand the conduct of intelligent people, because of their recklessness and their lack of forbearance. This is a possible reading.

The word al-Hujurat is the plural of hujr, and hujr is the plural of hujrah.

﴿And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them﴾. There are two interpretations:

First: It would have been better for their manners in obeying God and His Messenger (ﷺ).

Second: You would have released their captives without ransom, because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had taken captive some people from the Banu al-'Anbar, and they came seeking the ransom for their captives and prisoners.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 49, verses 6–8:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿O you who have believed, if there comes to you a deviator with information, verify it﴾ — the verse.

This verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt. The occasion of its revelation is what Sa'id narrated from Qatada (p. 329): "The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqba to collect the alms (musaddiqan) of the Banu al-Mustaliq. When they saw him, they came toward him, but he was afraid of them, so he returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him that they had apostatized from Islam. The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) then sent Khalid ibn al-Walid and instructed him to be steadfast and not to hasten. Khalid set out until he came to them at night and sent his scouts. When they came back, they informed Khalid that they were holding firmly to Islam, and they heard their call to prayer and their prayers. When morning came, Khalid went to them and saw the truth of what they had described, so they returned to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, and this verse was revealed."

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "Deliberation is from Allah, and haste is from Satan." In this verse there is evidence that the report of a single narrator (khabar al-wahid) is accepted when he is trustworthy ('adl).

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah. Were he to obey you in much of the matter, you would surely be in difficulty﴾ — concerning it there are five interpretations:

The first: you would surely sin (la-athimtum), said by Muqatil.

The second: you would surely be accused (la-ittahamtum), said by al-Kalbi.

The third: you would surely go astray (la-ghawaytum).

The fourth: you would surely perish (la-halaktum).

The fifth: hardship and difficulty would befall you (la-nalatkum shiddatun wa mashaqqatun).

Qatada said: These are the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ); were he to obey them in much of the matter, they would surely be in difficulty. By Allah, you are more foolish in judgment and more feeble-minded.

﴿But Allah has endeared to you the faith﴾ — concerning it there are two aspects:

The first: He made it beautiful to you, said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: said by al-Hasan:

by what He described of the reward for it.

﴿And has made it beautiful in your hearts﴾ — concerning it there are two aspects:

The first: by what He promised for it in this world of victory and in the Hereafter of reward, said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: by the proofs of its truth.

﴿And has made hateful to you disbelief, defiance, and disobedience﴾ — concerning it there are two aspects:

The first: that it refers specifically to lying, said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: everything that departs from obedience. (p. 330)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 49, verses 9–10:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, then make reconciliation between them﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are four opinions:

The first: what ʿAṭāʾ ibn Dīnār narrated from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, that "between the Aws and the Khazraj, during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), there was fighting with palm-stalks, sandals and the like, and this verse was revealed concerning them."

The second: what Saʿīd narrated from Qatadah, that it was revealed concerning two men from the Ansar who had a dispute over a right between them. One of them said to the other, "I will certainly take it from you by force, because of the multitude of my kin." The other invited him to bring their case before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but he refused to follow him. The matter continued between them until they clashed and each struck the other with hands and sandals, and this verse was revealed concerning them.

The third: what Asbāṭ narrated from al-Suddī, that a man of the Ansar had a wife called Umm Zayd. The woman wished to visit her family, but her husband detained her and placed her in an upper chamber of his, where no one of her family could enter to her. The woman sent word to her family, and her people came and brought her down so that they might take her away. The man went out and sought help from his family, and his paternal cousins came to prevent the woman from reaching her people. They pushed one another and fought with sandals, and this verse was revealed concerning them.

The fourth: what al-Kalbī, Muqātil and al-Farrāʾ related, that it was revealed concerning the company of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl of the Khazraj and the company of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah of the Aws. Its cause was that "the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by on his donkey to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy while he was in the assembly of his people, and the Prophet's donkey defecated, so ʿAbd Allāh pinched his nose and said, 'Away with your donkey!' ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah became angry and said, 'Do you say this about the donkey of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? By Allah, it is better smelling than you and your father!' His people became angry (p-331), and his people aided Ibn Rawāḥah until they fought with hands and sandals, and this verse was revealed concerning them. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made reconciliation between them."

﴿And if one of them transgresses against the other﴾. Baghy (transgression) is overstepping by force in seeking what is not one's due.

﴿Then fight against the one that transgresses﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: it transgresses by overstepping in the fighting.

The second: it transgresses by deviating from reconciliation; this is said by al-Farrāʾ.

﴿Until it returns to the command of Allah﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: it returns to the reconciliation which Allah commanded; this is said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

The second: it returns to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger concerning what is for them and against them; this is said by Qatadah.

﴿And if it returns﴾, i.e., it comes back.

﴿Then make reconciliation between them with justice﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: meaning with what is right.

The second: with the Book of Allah; this is said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

﴿And act justly﴾. Its meaning is: be even-handed.

It may bear two interpretations:

One: be even-handed by abandoning desire and partiality.

The second: by abandoning punishment and retribution.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves the just﴾, i.e., the even-handed. Abū Mālik said: in speech and in action.

The third: what Asbāṭ narrated from al-Suddī, that a man of the Ansar had a wife called Umm Zayd. The woman wished to visit her family, but her husband detained her and placed her in an upper chamber of his, where no one of her family could enter to her. The woman sent word to her family, and her people came and brought her down so that they might take her away. The man went out and sought help from his family, and his paternal cousins came to prevent the woman from reaching her people. They pushed one another and fought with sandals, and this verse was revealed concerning them.

The fourth: what al-Kalbī, Muqātil and al-Farrāʾ related, that it was revealed concerning the company of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl of the Khazraj and the company of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah of the Aws. Its cause was that "the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by on his donkey to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy while he was in the assembly of his people, and the Prophet's donkey defecated, so ʿAbd Allāh pinched his nose and said, 'Away with your donkey!' ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah became angry and said, 'Do you say this about the donkey of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? By Allah, it is better smelling than you and your father!' His people became angry (p-331), and his people aided Ibn Rawāḥah until they fought with hands and sandals, and this verse was revealed concerning them. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made reconciliation between them."

﴿And if one of them transgresses against the other﴾. Baghy (transgression) is overstepping by force in seeking what is not one's due.

﴿Then fight against the one that transgresses﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: it transgresses by overstepping in the fighting.

The second: it transgresses by deviating from reconciliation; this is said by al-Farrāʾ.

﴿Until it returns to the command of Allah﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: it returns to the reconciliation which Allah commanded; this is said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

The second: it returns to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger concerning what is for them and against them; this is said by Qatadah.

﴿And if it returns﴾, i.e., it comes back.

﴿Then make reconciliation between them with justice﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: meaning with what is right.

The second: with the Book of Allah; this is said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

﴿And act justly﴾. Its meaning is: be even-handed.

It may bear two interpretations:

One: be even-handed by abandoning desire and partiality.

The second: by abandoning punishment and retribution.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves the just﴾, i.e., the even-handed. Abū Mālik said: in speech and in action.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 49, verse 11:

As for "qawm" (people), it refers specifically to men; therefore, after mentioning them, He mentioned women.

Men are called "qawm" because some of them stand together with others in matters, and because they take charge of affairs without women. From this is the saying of the poet:

"I do not know, and I suppose I will never know, whether the people of Hisn are men (qawm) or women (nisa')."

Regarding this forbidden mockery (sukhriyyah), there are two opinions:

The first: it is the mockery of the wealthy toward the poor when the latter asks him. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it is the mockery of a Muslim toward one who has openly declared his sinfulness. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

A third possibility is that it is the mockery of the cunning toward the people of safety (ahl al-salamah).

﴿Perhaps they are better than them﴾ in the sight of Allah, the Exalted.

It may also mean: better than them in belief, and more sound inwardly.

﴿Nor let some women mock other women, for they may be better than them. And do not defame one another﴾. Regarding this, there are two aspects:

The first: do not defame the people of your religion.

The second: do not defame one another. Al-lamz (defamation) means finding fault.

Regarding its meaning here, there are three aspects:

The first: none of you should attack another. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: do not act deceitfully, so that some of you betray others. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: none of you should curse another. This was said by al-Dahhak.

﴿And do not insult one another with nicknames﴾. Regarding al-nabz (insult), there are two aspects:

The first: that it is a fixed nickname, said by al-Mubarrad.

The second: that al-nabz is an ugly statement, and regarding it here there are four aspects:

The first: that it is assigning a disliked nickname to a man and calling him by it.

Al-Sha'bi said: It was narrated that a delegation of Banu Sulaym came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and one of the men among them had two or three names, and he would call the man by a name, and it would be said that he disliked this, so this verse was revealed.

The second: that it is naming a man after his evil deeds after accepting Islam.

"O sinner!"

"O thief! O adulterer!" This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: that he reproaches him after Islam for the polytheism he had previously practiced. This was said by Ikrimah.

The fourth: that one calls a person, after his conversion to Islam, by the name of his religion before Islam, as for those Jews who had converted.

"O Jew!" and from the Christians:

"O Christian!" This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan.

As for preferred and admirable nicknames, they are not disliked, and the Prophet (ﷺ) described a number of his companions with attributes that became among the finest of titles for them.

There is disagreement about who this verse was revealed concerning, in four sayings:

The first: that it "was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, who had a heaviness in his hearing, so he would draw close to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that he could hear his speech. One day he came when people had taken their seats and said: 'Make room,' and they did, except for a man who was before the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not make room, and [Thabit] said: 'You have found a place,' and Thabit insulted him with a nickname that was disliked for his mother, so it was revealed." This was said by al-Kalbi and al-Farra'.

The second: that it was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn Malik al-Ansari, who was in charge of the spoils, and he said to Abd Allah ibn Abi Hadrad: "O bedouin!" and Abd Allah said to him: "O Jew!" and they complained of this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this was revealed concerning both of them. Related by Muqatil.

The third: that it was revealed concerning those who called out to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from behind the chambers, mocking those with the Messenger of Allah who were poor and clients, so this was revealed concerning them.

The fourth: that it was revealed concerning Aisha, when she found fault with Umm Salamah.

They differed regarding what she found fault with her for. Muqatil said she found fault with her shortness, and others said she found fault with a garment in which she had made a show.

...the Muslim, [based on] a suspicion without you knowing it with certainty.

﴿Indeed, some suspicion is sin.﴾ On this there are two views:

First: it means the suspicion of evil.

Second: that one speaks of what one suspects, and so it becomes sin. If one does not speak of it, it is not sin. This is the view of Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

﴿And do not spy.﴾ On this there are two views:

First: it is to follow the faults of the believer. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada.

Second: it is searching for what is hidden until it becomes apparent. This is the view of al-Awza'i.

Regarding *tajassus* (spying) and *tahassus* (seeking information) there are two views:

First: their meaning is one and the same. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan recited it with the letter *ḥā'* (*tahassus*).

The poet said:

"Su'da avoided mentioning her when you visit Su'da, [when] the hidden enemy is spying."

Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani said: "The *jāsūs* (spy) is the confidant of evil, and the *nāmūs* is the confidant of good."

Second: the two are different. Regarding the distinction between them there are two views:

First: *tajassus* with the letter *jīm* is searching, and from it it is said, "a man is a *jāsūs*" when he searches into matters. With the letter *ḥā'*, it is what a person perceives through one of his senses.

Second: with *ḥā'* it is that one seeks something for oneself, and with *jīm* it is that one acts as an agent for others.

*Tajassus* is that one seeks out news for oneself and for others.

﴿And do not backbite one another.﴾ *Ghībah* (backbiting) is mentioning a fault of someone in his absence. Al-Hasan said: "Backbiting is of three kinds, all of which are in the Book of God: *ghībah*, *ifk* (slander), and *buhtān* (false accusation). As for *ghībah*, it is that you say about your brother what is in him. As for *ifk*, it is that you say about him what has reached you about him. As for *buhtān*, it is that you say about him what is not in him."

Al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about backbiting, and he said: 'It is that you say to your brother what is in him. If you are truthful, then you have backbitten him, and if you are lying, then you have slandered him.'"

﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?﴾ On this there are two views:

First: meaning, just as it is forbidden to eat his flesh when dead, so backbiting him while alive is forbidden.

Second: just as one of you refrains from eating the flesh of his dead brother, so likewise he must refrain from backbiting him while alive. This is the view of Qatada.

He used the eating of flesh in place of backbiting because the custom of the Arabs runs along these lines. The poet said:

"If they eat my flesh, I shall nourish their flesh; and if they demolish my glory, I shall build for them glory."

﴿You would detest it.﴾ On this there are two views:

First: you detest eating carrion, so likewise detest backbiting.

Second: you detest that people should know of you [your faults], so detest people's backbiting [of you].

Then He said: ﴿And We made you nations and tribes that you may know one another.﴾ He thereby clarified that the nations and tribes are for mutual acquaintance, not for boasting. In this there are three views.

(p-336) The first: the "nations" (shu'ub) are the more distant lineage and the "tribes" (qaba'il) are the closer lineage. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The poet said:

Tribes out of nations, among whom there is no noble man who is counted or who is answered.

They were called shu'ub because the tribes branched out (tasha''aba) from them.

The second: the "nations" are the Arabs of Yemen descended from Qahtan, and the "tribe" is Rabi'ah, Mudar, and the rest of 'Adnan.

The third: the "nations" are the clans of the non-Arabs ('ajam), and the "tribes" are the clans of the Arabs.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: the "nations" are those attributed to regions and mountain passes, and the "tribes" are those who share in lineages. The poet said:

And they scattered into shu'ub, so every island has in it a commander of the believers and a pulpit.

The word shu'ub is the plural of sha'b with a fatha on the shin, while ash-sha'b with a kasra on the shin means "the path," and its plural is sh'ab. The difference between the two plurals, despite the similarity of the two words, is an alert to the difference in meaning.

﴿Indeed, the most honorable of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.﴾ Indeed, the most excellent of you. Honor comes through deeds and piety, not through lineage.

God the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted'"﴾. Regarding this, there are three interpretations:

The first: they affirmed (with their tongues) but did not act. Thus islam (submission) is speech and iman (faith) is action. This was said by al-Zuhri.

The second: they wished to take for themselves the name of the emigration (hijrah) before they had emigrated, so He informed them that their name is "Bedouins." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: they bestowed favour upon the Messenger of God by their Islam, saying, "We have submitted; we did not fight you." So God the Exalted said to His Prophet: "Say to them: You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted,' out of fear of the sword." This was said by Qatadah.

[This is] because they had believed with their tongues without their hearts, so they were not believers. And they abandoned fighting, so they became those who submit (mustaslimun) rather than those who are Muslims (muslimun). Thus the word is derived from istislam (submission) and not from islam, as the poet said:

"The day has grown long for one who has no milk-camel, except for the gift, or abandonment through islam."

On this interpretation, islam and iman are one in the ruling of the religion, and this is the position of the jurists (fuqaha'), because each of them is tasdiq (affirmation) and action.

They differ in two respects:

The first: in the root of the two names, for iman is derived from amn (security), and islam is derived from silm (peace).

The second: islam is the proper name for the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), while iman applies to all religions. For this reason, Jews and Christians refrained from calling themselves Muslims, but they did not refrain from calling themselves believers (mu'minun).

Al-Farra' said: This verse was revealed concerning the Bedouins of the clan of Bani Asad.

God the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿He will not deprive you of anything of your deeds﴾. Regarding this, there are two interpretations:

The first: He will not withhold from you any of the reward of your deeds. Ru'bah said:

"And a night of travel I journeyed, and the night of its journey did not hold me back from it."

That is, it did not prevent me from its journey.

The second: He will not diminish from the reward of your deeds anything. Al-Hutay'ah said:

"Convey to the nobles of Bani Sa'd a message, delivering the full effort of the message, without any diminishing or any lie."

That is, without any diminishing or any lie.

Regarding this, there are two readings: ﴿yalitkum﴾ and ya'litkum. Regarding these, there are two interpretations:

The first: they are two dialects with one meaning.

The second: ya'litkum is more frequent and more emphatic than yalitkum.

God the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Say: Do you inform God about your religion?﴾ and so on.

These are Bedouins around Madinah who showed Islam out of fear, and concealed polytheism in belief. So God manifested what they had concealed and uncovered what they had hidden, and by His knowledge of what is in the heavens and the earth He indicated a knowledge of what they believed. They had bestowed favour upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) by their Islam, and said, "We were preferred over others by our Islam, willingly."

So God the Exalted said: ﴿They bestow favour upon you that they have submitted. Say: Do not bestow favour upon me by your Islam﴾. This is correct, because if their Islam was true, then it is for the deliverance of their own souls, so there is no favour in it for them; and if it was hypocrisy, then it is for warding off harm from them, so the favour in it is upon them.

Then He said: ﴿Rather, God bestows favour upon you that He guided you to iman﴾. This admits of two interpretations:

The first: that God is more entitled to bestow favour upon you by guiding you to faith, so that you believed; and the favour here is the praise for the blessing.

The second: that God the Exalted bestows His blessing upon you by His guidance to you; and the favour here is the blessing itself.

The word "favour" (minnah) is sometimes used to express blessing, and sometimes to express praising for it.

﴿If you are truthful﴾ means: in what you said of faith.

The third: they bestowed favour upon the Messenger of God by their Islam, saying, "We have submitted; we did not fight you." So God the Exalted said to His Prophet: "Say to them: You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted,' out of fear of the sword." This was said by Qatadah.

[This is] because they had believed with their tongues without their hearts, so they were not believers. And they abandoned fighting, so they became those who submit (mustaslimun) rather than those who are Muslims (muslimun). Thus the word is derived from istislam (submission) and not from islam, as the poet said:

"The day has grown long for one who has no milk-camel, except for the gift, or abandonment through islam."

On this interpretation, islam and iman are one in the ruling of the religion, and this is the position of the jurists (fuqaha'), because each of them is tasdiq (affirmation) and action.

They differ in two respects:

The first: in the root of the two names, for iman is derived from amn (security), and islam is derived from silm (peace).

The second: islam is the proper name for the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), while iman applies to all religions. For this reason, Jews and Christians refrained from calling themselves Muslims, but they did not refrain from calling themselves believers (mu'minun).

Al-Farra' said: This verse was revealed concerning the Bedouins of the clan of Bani Asad.

God the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿He will not deprive you of anything of your deeds﴾. Regarding this, there are two interpretations:

The first: He will not withhold from you any of the reward of your deeds. Ru'bah said:

"And a night of travel I journeyed, and the night of its journey did not hold me back from it."

That is, it did not prevent me from its journey.

The second: He will not diminish from the reward of your deeds anything. Al-Hutay'ah said:

"Convey to the nobles of Bani Sa'd a message, delivering the full effort of the message, without any diminishing or any lie."

That is, without any diminishing or any lie.

Regarding this, there are two readings: ﴿yalitkum﴾ and ya'litkum. Regarding these, there are two interpretations:

The first: they are two dialects with one meaning.

The second: ya'litkum is more frequent and more emphatic than yalitkum.

God the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Say: Do you inform God about your religion?﴾ and so on.

These are Bedouins around Madinah who showed Islam out of fear, and concealed polytheism in belief. So God manifested what they had concealed and uncovered what they had hidden, and by His knowledge of what is in the heavens and the earth He indicated a knowledge of what they believed. They had bestowed favour upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) by their Islam, and said, "We were preferred over others by our Islam, willingly."

So God the Exalted said: ﴿They bestow favour upon you that they have submitted. Say: Do not bestow favour upon me by your Islam﴾. This is correct, because if their Islam was true, then it is for the deliverance of their own souls, so there is no favour in it for them; and if it was hypocrisy, then it is for warding off harm from them, so the favour in it is upon them.

Then He said: ﴿Rather, God bestows favour upon you that He guided you to iman﴾. This admits of two interpretations:

The first: that God is more entitled to bestow favour upon you by guiding you to faith, so that you believed; and the favour here is the praise for the blessing.

The second: that God the Exalted bestows His blessing upon you by His guidance to you; and the favour here is the blessing itself.

The word "favour" (minnah) is sometimes used to express blessing, and sometimes to express praising for it.

﴿If you are truthful﴾ means: in what you said of faith.
